fields.title: Zvod: Decision Made to Shut Down Business Unit
fields.summary: Fifteen hundred clients will find out from you. Decide how to organize everything.
fields.decisionPrompt: How will you plan the unit shutdown?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager for Zvod.Smeta.
fields.brief/company: Zvod is a fictional company building tools for construction contractors. The main product is project management; Zvod.Smeta is a separate cost estimation unit.
fields.brief/context: The board decided to close Smeta: 1,480 paying clients after three years against a plan of 6,000. The unit costs four developers and is unprofitable. Shutdown date is in five months. How to announce and what to do next is undecided.
fields.brief/constraints: Five months until shutdown. Four developers and two support staff are assigned to the unit.
fields.brief/task: Choose a plan and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Shutdown is work, not pulling the plug
fields.learnTakeaway/body: You can close a product so that people speak well of you, or so that it gets brought up for years whenever choosing a vendor. The difference lies in four things: telling people in advance, giving back their data, refunding money, and suggesting what to do next. And in the order: the team finds out first, otherwise there will be no one left to support the sunsetting product in its final months.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
1,480 paying users, average check 4,200 ₽ per month.

Of these, 620 also use Zvod's main product.

210 clients in Smeta have more than three hundred estimates — that's years of work; an estimate contains rates, templates, and revision history.

Export is currently available only to its own internal format, which no one else can read. Exporting to a standard format takes 3 weeks of work.

340 clients have paid a year in advance, with an average of 7 months remaining.

The builders' industry community has about 15 thousand people; Smeta's clients are active there, discussing tools and recommending them to each other.

Two competitors in the estimate market: one is more expensive and powerful, the second is comparable in price.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Four developers, two support staff, a quarter-time designer.

Three developer vacancies are open in the main product.

Four people know about the decision: the board, you, the CFO. The team does not know.

Rumors have already started: two developers asked you last week if it's true the unit is closing.

Smeta support knows clients by name: two have worked with them for three years.

One developer is the only person who understands the calculation core.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
CFO: shut down on the date, notify clients a month prior—"if we tell them earlier, they'll leave earlier and stop paying."

CCO: try selling the unit to one of the two competitors; negotiations will take 2–3 months, outcome unknown.

One of the PMs: move to maintenance mode without updates and "let it live as long as they pay."

Founder is concerned about reputation: "construction is a tight circle, word spreads."

Lawyer: for early service termination, prepaid amounts must be refunded; total for 340 clients is noticeable but manageable.

No option has been calculated in terms of money and timeline yet.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
A year ago, a competitor closed a similar service: shut down with two weeks' notice, provided no export.

It was discussed in the trade community for a month; some affected users still bring up this story when choosing a vendor.

Zvod's main product is sold to the same contractors, often the same individuals.

Last year, Zvod already moved the sunset date for an old version of its main product twice; announced dates are now trusted less.

Smeta support receives about 90 tickets per week; a surge is expected upon announcement.

When switching to a competitor, a client needs to transfer pricing and templates—manually, this takes days of work per client.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Exit as planned: team first, then clients, with data and a firm date
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Tell the team on day one, announce to clients immediately with a date, build standard format export, refund prepayments, and suggest migration options.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
You talk to the team on day one: rumors are already spreading, and silence destroys trust faster than bad news. You offer three developers open roles in the main product, and agree with the core engine developer to stay until shutdown for a retention bonus.
You write to clients in week two—four and a half months out, not one month. You check the CFO's argument about "they'll stop paying": churn indeed accelerates after the announcement, but refunding prepayments was inevitable anyway, and reputation is worth more.
You build export to a standard format in three weeks—the single thing 210 clients with hundreds of estimates will remember you for.
You offer an honest comparison of two competitors: which one suits whom. 380 clients switch to one of them, and 290 of those using both products stay with the main one.
You never move the date—after two previous delays, this matters.
Discussion in the trade community happens, but the tone is neutral; three users publicly post that advance notice and data export were provided.
Trade-off: five months of supporting a sunsetting unit and refunding prepayments cost noticeable money, requiring defense before the CFO.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The CFO is right: the earlier we tell them, the earlier they stop paying. Announce a month before, shut down on schedule.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
One month is less than a client with 300 estimates needs to migrate their work.
There is no export to a standard format, and building it in a month alongside a ticket surge fails.
In the trade community, the story spreads in a week and is discussed for over a month, compared to the competitor's incident last year.
Sales of the main product to the same contractors become harder: in three deals, clients ask "won't you close this in a year too?"
The team finds out about the shutdown almost simultaneously with clients; the core calculation engine developer leaves two weeks later, and the final month of support hangs by a thread.
Trade-off: saved a few months of payments at the cost of reputation in a tight market where the main product is sold.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Try selling the business unit first
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The CCO suggests negotiating with a competitor: clients transfer along with the product, avoiding offboarding.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
This is a reasonable alternative to closing, and worth exploring—but negotiations take 2–3 months out of five, during which nothing can be announced.
Team rumors turn into certainty over two months; two developers leave on their own.
The deal falls through: the competitor wants the clients, not the code.
Two months remain for offboarding instead of five, nobody is left to build export, and everything degrades into a rushed shutdown.
Trade-off: valid alternative explored without a parallel offboarding plan, consuming time needed by clients when it failed.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Shift to maintenance mode without active development
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Clients are paying, closing feels wasteful. Leave as is, downsize team to one person, stop developing.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
Formally nothing happens, avoiding an uncomfortable conversation.
Six months later, incompatibilities stack up: pricing regulations change, but no one is around to update them.
Clients discover this themselves in the middle of work and leave feeling quietly deceived.
The community adopts the phrase "Zvod abandoned Smeta but keeps taking money"—worse than an honest shutdown.
The single support person burns out and leaves, triggering an unmanaged emergency shutdown without any plan.
Trade-off: decision deferred rather than made; shutdown happens anyway, in the worst possible way and without preparation.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Acquisition plan relies on a single channel without reserve or capacity knowledge
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Retention reduced to mechanics instead of processes with an owner and metric
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Launch reduced to an announcement date without decisions on segment, promise, and success
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Business unit closure lacks a plan for offboarding people and data
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: External communication evaluated by incoming requests and unprepared for bad news
